transcript.note: Loop round 1. Compaction only removes a band that is COMPLETELY empty, so instead of proposing moves segment by segment I inventoried which columns and rows are held open by a single station, and asked for each of those whether that station can be slid onto an ALREADY-OCCUPIED band without breaking any of its axial segments. That is the whole method this round: every move below is along a station's own free axis, so all 60 H/V segments are preserved by construction. Columns freed this way: 5 (11 slid east along row 40 onto column 7, which already holds 43/56/57), 12 (29 slid west along row 52 onto the same column 7), 19 (42 slid east along row 42 onto column 23, which also shortens that route by four cells), 24 (0 is a leaf on a 45-degree segment, so I moved it one cell along that same 45-degree ray to (25,15), which keeps the diagonal exactly and lands it on both an occupied column and an occupied row, freeing row 14 as well), 41 (5 slid east along row 9 onto column 43 — shorter too), 54 and 56 (41 slid one cell east onto 54's column and 46 one cell east onto column 57; I checked the alternative of moving 54 and keeping 46, which frees the same two columns but needs longer moves). Rows freed: 8 (4, 35 and 37 all moved one cell north onto row 9, which is already occupied by 5 and 6 — this is a rigid one-row shift of the whole row-8 population, so 4-35 stays H, 35-45 stays V and 18-37 stays V), 0 (47 moved up column 3 to row 1; the key point is that 4 stayed on column 11, so the 8/8 diagonal 4-47 is still exactly 45 degrees — moving 4 as well would have broken it), 3 and 4 (the leaves 21 and 14 slid along their own vertical segments onto occupied rows 6, which also shortens both), 20 (48 is a pass-through on column 0 between 14 and 7, so it can sit on any row between them; row 23 is already occupied), 37 (55 is the same kind of pass-through on column 57 and moved onto row 33), 50 (19 slid down its vertical onto row 52). I deliberately did NOT touch 33 (row 26) or 38 (row 13): each is the unique cell that keeps two 45-degree segments exact, and freeing those rows would cost more than the row is worth. Likewise 36 and 39 could each free a column by sliding along their horizontals, but only at the price of a 45-degree segment, so I left them. Expected result: 26 occupied columns and 26 occupied rows before compaction become 19 and 18.

Loop round 2. Compaction has nothing left to take — there are now zero empty bands — so the only way to shrink further is to CREATE an empty band, and the candidates are the bands held open by exactly one station: columns 3, 8, 10 and rows 4, 8. I evaluated each by asking what it costs. (a) Column 3 holds only 4. Sliding 4 west onto the occupied column 2 keeps 4-35 horizontal but would flatten the 4-47 diagonal, because 47 is nailed to column 1 by its vertical to 8. The fix is to move the ROW instead: 4 to (2,1) and its partner 35 to (5,1) together, a rigid one-row lift that keeps 4-35 horizontal, keeps 35-45 vertical (35 stays on column 5), and lands 4 exactly one cell diagonally from 47 so the 45-degree segment survives. Row 2 stays occupied by 5, 6 and 37, so nothing is lost. (b) Column 10 holds only 39, which is a pass-through on row 12 between 42 and 25; sliding it east onto column 11 keeps both horizontals and frees the column outright, at no cost. (c) Row 8 holds only 33, a pass-through on column 5 between 45 and 15, so it may sit on any row between them. Rather than picking the nearest occupied row I solved for the row that also fixes something: at (5,9) BOTH of its skew segments become exact 45-degree segments at once — 33-43 becomes 3/3 and 16-33 becomes 1/1 — so this move frees a row and repairs two segments simultaneously. I verified that lengthening 45-33 to three cells does not cross any horizontal, since rows 7 and 8 carry nothing west of column 11. (d) I left row 4 alone: 38 could slide down its vertical to free it, but 38 currently satisfies three of its four edges and two of those are 45-degree segments that the slide would destroy. (e) I also left column 8 alone: 36 could slide west to free it, but only by giving up the 45-degree segment to 45, and 36 cannot go further west without its horizontal to 44 crossing the vertical 15-33 on column 5.

Loop round 3. Same inventory method, but this round I stopped looking only at bands held open by ONE station and started looking at bands held open by a rigid PAIR that can move together. (a) Column 7 holds only 36. Compaction had already flattened the 45-degree segment 45-36 into a 3/2 skew, so sliding 36 one cell west along its horizontal now costs nothing — and at (6,8) it is exactly 2/2 from 45, so the 45-degree segment comes back. Freeing a column and repairing a segment with one move. (b) Column 10 is held by the pair 2 and 3, joined by a vertical: 2 is a pass-through on row 3 between 18 and 13 and 3 is a leaf on row 0, so the pair can slide sideways as a rigid unit to any column in 9..12 without disturbing anything. Column 9 is already occupied, so I moved both there; I checked that the lengthened 13-2 horizontal does not clip 38, whose vertical starts one row below it. (c) Row 12 is held by the pair 31 and 32, joined by a horizontal, each hanging off a vertical from above; lifting both one row onto the occupied row 11 keeps the horizontal and both verticals. (d) Row 5 is held by 0, 53 and 54. 53 is a pass-through on column 14 above 22 and can sit on row 6; 54 is its leaf partner and follows to keep their horizontal; 0 is a leaf whose only segment is skew, and I checked it cannot go onto row 6 because every cell there between columns 4 and 8 lies on the 45-20 horizontal and would be swallowed — so I sent it the other way to row 4, where its segment to 20 becomes an exact 2/2 diagonal. Three moves, one row freed and a segment repaired. I am still leaving row 4's other occupant 38 alone: it satisfies three of its four edges, two of them at 45 degrees, and every alternative cell on its column satisfies only one.

Loop round 4. Two group moves, both of which need their members to travel together. (a) Row 9 carries the whole western horizontal chain 7-11-15 and nothing else, so the only way to free it is to lift all three onto an occupied row at once. Row 8 works: 15 is pinned to column 4 by its vertical to 33 but is free to slide north along it, and 7 is pinned to column 0 by its vertical to 48 in the same way, so the lift preserves both verticals and both horizontals of the chain. The payoff is bigger than a row: 16 sits at (5,8), so once 15 arrives at (4,8) the segment 16-15 stops being 45 degrees and becomes a true horizontal — the first H/V gain of the loop. (b) Column 1 carries only the pair 47 and 8, but they could not simply shift east because 4 was sitting on the landing cell (2,1). So this is a three-body move: 4 steps one column east to (3,1), which keeps its horizontal to 35 and, crucially, leaves it exactly one cell diagonally from 47's new home, so the 4-47 45-degree segment survives; 8 and 47 then take the vacated column 2. I relied on the applier's multi-pass behaviour here — the first pass may reject a member whose partner has not moved yet, and the later passes pick it up. I again left row 4 (0 and 38) and column 13 (41 and 54) alone: 38 would have to give up two 45-degree segments to leave its row, and 41 cannot leave column 13 because the only cell east of it on its row lies inside 34's vertical and would be swallowed.

Loop round 5. The grid cannot shrink further without paying for it, so this round is about the fourth loop goal — shorter routes — and about the four segments still not aligned. (a) 36 sat at the one cell of its horizontal that kept an exact 45-degree segment to 45, but that single diagonal was costing it TWO skew segments (to 23 and to 58). Moving it one cell east to (6,7) inverts the trade: 36-23 and 36-58 both become 1/1 diagonals and only 45-36 degrades, so it is two gained for one given up, and all three of those segments get shorter at the same time. Its horizontal to 44 survives because the move is along row 7. (b) 39 is a pass-through on row 9 between 42 and 25, free to sit on any column in 5..7; column 5 is the one that puts it exactly one cell diagonally below 16, so 16-39 becomes a 1/1 diagonal — the last of the four offenders that could be closed at all. (c) On the grid: the only remaining band held by fewer than three stations that could still be emptied is row 4, and I verified it cannot be done cheaply — 0 can leave it while keeping its diagonal, but 38's quadrant constraints against 13 above and 12 below confine it to rows 4 and 5, and row 5 destroys both its 45-degree segments. One row out of fourteen is not worth two exact diagonals, so I am leaving it. Column 12 is likewise blocked for good: 41 cannot cross to the west of 30, and the only cell east of it lies inside 34's vertical, which no move can vacate because 55 is trapped between 34 and 32.
